anchor.title: Portrait of John Locke
anchor.creator: Sir Godfrey Kneller
anchor.caption: John Locke (1632–1704), whose Second Treatise of Government argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed — a direct root of American political thought.
anchor.alt: Painted portrait of John Locke, an English philosopher in dark robes, seated and facing slightly right.

anchor.title: Declaration of Independence (engrossed copy)
anchor.creator: Second Continental Congress; engrossed by Timothy Matlack
anchor.caption: The engrossed Declaration of Independence, 1776 — the document that turned the colonists' grievances into a claim of natural rights and self-government.
anchor.alt: Aged parchment of the Declaration of Independence with the bold heading and columns of signatures below the text.

anchor.title: Join, or Die
anchor.creator: Benjamin Franklin
anchor.caption: Franklin's 'Join, or Die' (1754): a severed snake labeled with the colonies. Under the loose Articles of Confederation, the states struggled to act as one — the cartoon's warning about disunity still fit.
anchor.alt: Woodcut of a snake cut into segments, each labeled with the initials of a colony, above the words JOIN, or DIE.
anchor.citation: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division · https://www.loc.gov/item/2002695523/

anchor.title: U.S. Constitution, Page 1 (“We the People”)
anchor.creator: Constitutional Convention; engrossed by Jacob Shallus
anchor.caption: The first page of the Constitution opens with the Preamble — 'We the People' — stating the purposes government exists to serve.
anchor.alt: First parchment page of the U.S. Constitution with the large opening words 'We the People' in ornate script.

anchor.title: The Federalist, Volume 1 (title page)
anchor.creator: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, John Jay ('Publius')
anchor.caption: The Federalist (1788). In No. 51, Madison argued that a government of separated, checking powers is necessary 'because men are not angels' — the logic of limited government.
anchor.alt: Printed 1788 title page reading 'THE FEDERALIST: A Collection of Essays' with publisher details below.
anchor.citation: Library of Congress, Rare Book & Special Collections · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Federalist_(1st_ed,_1788,_vol_I,_title_page).jpg

anchor.title: The Federal Edifice (“The Federal Pillars”)
anchor.creator: Massachusetts Centinel
anchor.caption: The 'Federal Pillars' cartoon (1788) shows states rising as columns of the new structure — a fitting image for the Constitution's architecture and its deliberately hard amendment process.
anchor.alt: Cartoon of classical columns, each labeled with a state, being raised to form the roof of a building labeled for the federal government.
anchor.citation: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division · https://www.loc.gov/item/2004676796/

anchor.title: The Bill of Rights (engrossed copy)
anchor.creator: 1st U.S. Congress
anchor.caption: The engrossed Bill of Rights, 1789. The first eight Amendments each draw a boundary government may not cross; the 9th and 10th reserve rights and powers to the people and the states.
anchor.alt: Parchment page listing the proposed Articles of amendment that became the Bill of Rights, in columns of handwritten text.

anchor.title: Great Seal of the United States (obverse)
anchor.creator: Charles Thomson & William Barton (design)
anchor.caption: The Great Seal's motto, E Pluribus Unum — 'out of many, one' — captures the constitutional republic: many states and citizens under one representative government limited by law.
anchor.alt: The obverse of the Great Seal of the United States: an eagle holding an olive branch and arrows, with a shield and a banner reading E Pluribus Unum.
anchor.citation: U.S. National Archives / public domain (U.S. government emblem) · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Great_Seal_of_the_United_States_(obverse).svg
